As discussed, attached are two small invoice simulations and a draft term sheet so we can align on three things we heard you worry about: 1) how token rounding and per-call minimums affect long-context sessions, 2) how context-length interacts with our staircase discounts if you commit, and 3) whether we can offer a short initial concession while you ramp.

Quick notes on attachments: invoice-sim-1.csv is a per-call rounding example (round up to 100-token quantum), invoice-sim-2.csv shows aggregated-per-session accounting (aggregate tokens per user session before rounding), and redwood-pricing-term-sheet-v2.pdf has the proposed commit tiers and discount breakpoints.

As next steps, can you confirm two data points so we can pick the appropriate simulation to finalize pricing:
- Typical session distribution (how many requests per session, and rough median session length).
- Expected monthly committed tokens if you were to consider a 3‑month pilot / 12‑month commit.

If you want, Dylan (copied) can run a custom simulation against a sample export of your token logs — even a single week's webhook sample would be enough.

Hi Soojin —

Appreciate the sims. A couple clarifying questions before we ask procurement to review:

1) For a scenario where we see ~100k tokens/day but 75–80% of that traffic is from very long sessions (50k–120k tokens/session), does your per-call minimum apply per inference call or per user session? If per call, the rounding to a 100-token quantum could be material.

2) How do you treat streaming responses for long-history retrievals? Do you meter the full reconstructed prompt+history and round at the same quantum, or only the tokens emitted?

3) Can you show a worked example where rounding and minimums increase charges vs. an aggregation-per-session approach? We want to understand the delta for our finance/forecasting.

We can share a small export (anonymized) if needed. Procurement prefers to see the worst-case monthly invoice simulation before committing.

Thanks,

Elena —

Thanks for the questions. Below are three worked simulations (text summary — full CSVs attached in the original from Soojin). I kept the math conservative. Assumptions: base rate $0.00030 / token (hosted), rounding quantum 100 tokens unless aggregated, per-call minimum equivalent to 100 tokens, streaming responses meter total prompt+response tokens.

1) Naive per-call rounding (worst case)
- Daily activity: 100,000 tokens total
- Traffic composition: 80% long sessions (80k tokens), split into 2 calls/session on average (40k tokens each) → each call rounded to nearest 100, no aggregation
- Rounding overhead: 2 calls * rounding up 40k to 40,000 (no uplift if exact) but smaller calls produce more overhead — assume 6% extra tokens due to rounding in real logs
- Monthly estimate: 100k * 30 days = 3,000,000 billed tokens * 1.06 overhead = 3,180,000 billed tokens → $954.00/month

2) Aggregated-per-session before rounding (more favorable)
- Aggregate tokens per user session and round once per session. With same traffic, rounding overhead drops to ~0.8%
- Monthly billed tokens ≈ 3,024,000 → $907.20/month

3) Commit + staircase discounts (example tier)
- Proposed commit: 2,000,000 tokens/month at 12% discount (effective $0.000264 / token)
- Overage billed at standard rate with aggregated-per-session accounting
- Using the sample workload (3,000,000 tokens), you pay: committed 2,000,000 * $0.000264 = $528.00 + overage 1,000,000 * $0.00030 = $300.00 → $828.00/month (vs $954 naive)

Notes / operational options:
- We can configure server-side aggregation (session-based timers) so tokens are bucketed per session before rounding — this reduces rounding waste significantly for long-history retrievals.
- For streaming, our meter counts the total tokens reconstructed on the server side (prompt + response). We can optionally expose a streaming-only meter if you want to only pay for emitted tokens; that requires a small instrumentation change and a short pilot.
- If you provide a 7‑day export, I can run these sims against raw event data and return a per-user heatmap and a concrete delta between methods.

Happy to hop on a quick 30‑minute session to walk through the CSV outputs.

—Dylan

Subject: Proposal: pilot commit and initial concession (CC-4532)

Elena / Procurement —

Following Dylan's sims, here's a concrete proposal to make procurement's review easier:

Proposal summary:
- Pilot commit: 2,000,000 tokens / month for a 90‑day pilot, priced at 12% discount off list ($0.000264 / token).
- Accounting method: aggregated-per-session before rounding (this is what invoice-sim-2.csv models).
- Initial concession: Redwood will waive the per-call minimum rounding impact for the first invoice month and instead bill by aggregated-per-session for month one only. If you sign an annual commit within 30 days after the pilot, we'll convert the pilot month to a one-time credit instead of waiver.
- Staircase discounts: tiers at 2M (12%), 5M (18%), 10M+ (25%) — tier prices and examples in attached term sheet.

Why this helps: the waiver removes the immediate rounding noise so your finance team sees a clean first-month baseline. After that, the committed rate + aggregation reduces both charge volatility and absolute cost vs naive per-call rounding.

Next steps: if procurement is comfortable with the pilot numbers, we'll deliver a one-page SOW + DocuSign link (I can have legal/finance prep it by EOD). Deal reference CC-4532 sits on our side.

Thanks,
Soojin Lee
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
soojin.lee@redwood.com

2) We need the DocuSign envelope to include procurement@cloudcore.ai and legal@cloudcore.ai.
